label: Owner vs stakeholder vs approver in a change

mentor.diagnosis: You treated the person doing the work, the person accountable for the system, and the person authorising the change as interchangeable. The exam separates them deliberately, because the control only works when they are different people.
contrast: Role
What they are on the hook for
What they are NOT
Owner
The asset itself: it exists, it is classified, someone is accountable for it in the register
Not automatically the approver, and usually not the engineer
Stakeholder
Anyone the change affects, who must be consulted and informed
Not a veto, and not accountable for the outcome
Approver
Authorising the change to proceed, through CAB or a defined delegate
Not the implementer, or nobody independent reviewed it
Implementer
Executing the change inside the window, to the written plan
Not the person who approves their own work
mentor.rule: Owner is accountable for the asset, stakeholders are consulted about the change, the approver authorises it, and the implementer performs it. If one person is doing two of those, name the separation-of-duties problem.
mentor.tell: A stem naming several people around one change and asking whose sign-off is needed, or who must be informed.
mentor.trap: In small organisations these really are the same person, so the real-world answer and the exam answer diverge. The exam is asking what the process requires, not what your employer does.

label: What a change actually disturbs: restarts, dependencies, legacy systems and downtime

mentor.diagnosis: You judged the blast radius by the size of the change rather than by what has to stop and what depends on it. A one-line config edit that forces a service restart takes the service down exactly as hard as a rebuild does.
contrast: Implication
What it means
Why it bites
Service restart
A system service must be stopped and started for the change to take effect
Brief but total for anything depending on that service
Application restart
The application process is recycled, sessions are dropped
Users lose in-flight work even though the host never rebooted
Dependencies
Other systems rely on this one, often undocumented
The outage lands somewhere nobody listed on the change
Legacy applications
Unsupported or undocumented systems that may not survive the change
No vendor to call, and often no test environment to prove it first
Downtime
Planned unavailability agreed with the business
Unplanned downtime is the same technical event without the agreement
Restricted activities
Work the change explicitly does not authorise
Scope creep during a window is how one change becomes an incident
mentor.rule: Ask what must restart, what depends on it, and what the change does not authorise. Those three questions find most of the impact that an impact analysis misses.
mentor.tell: A change described as small, routine or low risk, where the stem then mentions a restart, an integration, or an old system.
mentor.trap: Low risk and low impact are not the same claim. A low risk change can still take a dependent system down, and the approval you needed was theirs.

label: What has to be updated after a change: diagrams, procedures and version control

mentor.diagnosis: You treated the change as finished when the system worked. The objectives put documentation inside change management because stale diagrams and procedures are what make the next incident longer.
contrast: Artefact
Updated when
What goes wrong if it is not
Network and system diagrams
Anything that moves, adds or removes a path
Responders fight the topology instead of the incident
Policies and procedures
The change alters how people are supposed to work
Staff follow a procedure that no longer matches the system
Version control
Every configuration or code change, as it is made
No way to see what changed, by whom, or to roll back cleanly
Standard operating procedure
A change becomes routine and repeatable
Every repeat is improvised and inconsistent
mentor.rule: The change is not complete when the system works. It is complete when the diagram, the procedure and the repository agree with the system.
mentor.tell: A question asking what remains outstanding after a successful implementation, or why a later incident took longer than it should have.
mentor.trap: Documentation reads like administrative tidiness, so it loses against answers that sound technical. On this objective it is the point: version control is also how the backout plan actually works.

label: Backout plan vs maintenance window vs impact analysis vs approval

mentor.diagnosis: You named the wrong element of the change process for what the scenario was actually missing.
contrast: Element
Answers
Missing when
Impact analysis
What will this change affect
Nobody realised the change would take the VPN down
Approval process
Who authorised this change
The engineer changed production alone
Test results
Did it work somewhere safe first
It was applied straight to production
Backout plan
How do we undo this if it goes wrong
The change failed and the team could not revert
Maintenance window
When may this be applied
The change ran at 10am on a trading day
Standard operating procedure
How is this kind of change normally done
Every engineer does it differently
mentor.rule: Match the element to the failure. Could not undo means backout plan. Wrong time means maintenance window. Unexpected side effect means impact analysis.
mentor.tell: 'The team was unable to restore service after the update failed' is a missing backout plan, every time.
mentor.trap: Approval is the element people name by reflex because it sounds like governance. Read which part of the change actually broke.
